title: Kashmiri Filmmaker Arfat Sheikh Released on Bond After Two Weeks in ICE Detention
excerpt: Sheikh was detained at Washington Dulles airport on September 24; the deportation case against him continues even as his film 'Saffron Kingdom' landed a US distribution deal.
body:
• Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh was released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention on bond on Thursday after two weeks in custody, according to a campaign of his friends and relatives.
  • Sheikh, 42, was detained by ICE on September 24 while coming off a plane from California at Washington Dulles International Airport; bond was granted on Tuesday, and the deportation case against him continues.
  • His supporters say he entered the US in 2019 on a student visa, studied film at Georgia State University, filed for asylum in 2020, and held work authorization while his immigration case was pending. The Department of Homeland Security says he overstayed his lawful admittance and that a pending application confers no legal status.
  • The detention drew international attention because of Sheikh's film "Saffron Kingdom," an award-winning feature about a Kashmiri family's experience of decades of conflict — which landed an exclusive US distribution deal while he was still in custody.

Arfat Sheikh, the award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained by US immigration authorities at Washington Dulles International Airport on September 24, was released on bond on Thursday after two weeks in ICE custody, according to the campaign pressing for his release. The deportation case against him continues.

Two weeks behind bars, released on bond

Sheikh was freed from the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia, after bond was granted on Tuesday, according to the Free Arfat Sheikh campaign. The 42-year-old, who lives in Alexandria, Virginia, entered the United States in 2019 on a student visa to study film at Georgia State University and filed for asylum in 2020, the campaign said. His supporters maintain he had a pending immigration application and was authorized to work and live in the US.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=_dZenZyrSvM

The Department of Homeland Security offered a different account. DHS said Sheikh was arrested on September 24, "legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance." A pending application does not confer legal status in the US, the department said, adding that he will receive due process.

"It appears they had advanced knowledge and they were waiting at the airport to take him into custody."

— Hassan Ahmad, Sheikh's lawyer, to the Kashmir Times

A detention supporters call unwarranted

Sheikh's lawyer, Hassan Ahmad, told the Kashmir Times that the detention appeared premeditated: ICE officers seemed to have advance knowledge and were waiting at the airport. Ahmad placed the case in the context of hundreds of ICE detentions since President Donald Trump took office, calling it unjust "to pick up people without any criminal record, without any reason, and spend taxpayers' money to keep them detained."

https://x.com/Reuters/status/2108413408588583321

"Today, in Arfat's case, a small amount of justice has been served."

— Hassan Ahmad, Sheikh's lawyer, to the Kashmir Times

According to supporters, Sheikh was traveling with author and filmmaker Tara Dorabji en route to an "Art as Resistance" panel in Washington, DC, when plainclothes agents detained him despite his presenting immigration paperwork. Dr. Ali Mohammed Mir, president of Daffodil Studios, which produced Sheikh's debut feature, told the Kashmir Times: "There is nothing against him."

The filmmaker and "Saffron Kingdom"

Sheikh's case has drawn attention far beyond immigration circles because of his work. His debut feature, "Saffron Kingdom," a deeply personal film about a Kashmiri family navigating decades of trauma, displacement, and resilience, has won Best Feature Film honors at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, the Melbourne Independent Film Festival, and several other festivals, plus the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the 2025 Teaneck International Film Festival. It has screened at more than 100 theaters, universities, and cultural institutions internationally, including Johns Hopkins, Syracuse, SOAS University of London, and the Australian National University.

While Sheikh was still in detention, "Saffron Kingdom" landed an exclusive US distribution deal with OMG! and The Black Network. The announcement, landing mid-detention rather than around it, turned the deal into a public stand by the distributors.

Sheikh's work is rooted in personal loss. In July 2003, his father Ghulam Nabi Sheikh, a celebrated Kashmiri singer, disappeared while traveling by train from Jammu to Delhi. The family alleged an enforced disappearance and killing; Arfat was 16 at the time.

Part of a wider crackdown

Sheikh's detention sits within the Trump administration's sweeping immigration enforcement drive. In August, the administration said it was working "to identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently." Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights, Reuters reported.

What happens next

Sheikh's release is not an exoneration — the deportation case against him continues, and DHS has said he will receive due process through the immigration court system. For now the filmmaker is out of custody; whether he remains in the country will be decided by the proceedings ahead.
